opus-5.5.text:
I think it's further away than a lot of people in San Francisco would guess, though probably not as far as skeptics think.

When people talk about a drop-in remote worker, they tend to picture the things models are already good at: writing code, answering questions, drafting documents. But being a useful remote worker involves much more than that. You need to hold context over weeks or months, coordinate with other people, notice when something has gone wrong and recover, decide what to work on when nobody has specified it, and handle the messy, under-specified parts of a job that never show up in a benchmark. That's where current systems are weakest. A lot of it is a kind of Moravec's paradox: what feels hard to us, like competition math or writing a function, turns out to be relatively easy, and what feels trivial, like competently running a multi-week project, turns out to be hard.

When I try to forecast this, I look at a few things. First, the trend in the length of tasks AI can complete autonomously. That has been growing quickly, maybe doubling every several months, but we're still mostly talking about tasks measured in hours, and real jobs are made of projects that span weeks. Extrapolating that curve gets you somewhere interesting, but there's real uncertainty about whether it holds as tasks get longer and less well defined.

Second, compute. Much of the progress we've seen comes from scaling training compute, and there are real constraints ahead on power, chips, and capital. I expect continued rapid scaling through the end of the decade, but at some point the growth rate has to slow, and if we haven't unlocked the key capabilities by then, timelines stretch out quite a bit.

Third, and this is underappreciated, the data and environments. We don't have large datasets of people doing full jobs end to end, with all the context, tool use, and feedback that involves. You need rich training environments that capture what real work looks like, and building those is a substantial, unglamorous effort.

Putting that together, my median for something you could genuinely hire in place of a typical remote knowledge worker, across most such jobs, is probably sometime in the 2030s, with a wide distribution. I'd put meaningful probability on it happening sooner, but I don't think the default is two or three years. And even once the capability exists, deployment and economic integration take time. The economy doesn't reorganize overnight just because a model can do something in principle.

r001.rationale: The response forecasts replacement across most typical remote knowledge-worker jobs, but it does not distinguish that scope from replacement on every remotely performable task.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that I put a fair amount of probability mass on this happening within something like the next decade, maybe a bit longer, but I want to be careful about what "drop-in remote worker" actually means, because I think people use that phrase to gesture at a few different things.

The strong version is something like: you can hire this system the way you'd hire a contractor, give it a laptop and a Slack login and a vague description of the job, and it just figures it out over weeks and months, builds context, handles the ambiguous stuff, follows up with people, notices when something's gone wrong that nobody asked it to look at. That's a very high bar. It's not really a capabilities question in the narrow sense of "can it do this task." It's a question about whether the system can operate autonomously over long horizons, with very sparse feedback, in an environment that wasn't designed for it.

And I think the thing that's been striking to me, looking at the data we've collected at Epoch, is that the length of tasks models can do reliably has been growing pretty fast, something like doubling every several months on the benchmarks we can measure. If you extrapolate that naively, you get to tasks that take humans weeks within a few years. But I'd flag two things. One, the benchmarks are cleaner than the real world. They're well-specified, they have a clear success criterion, and the environment is sandboxed. Real jobs have a lot of what I'd call "unobserved" difficulty, where the hard part is figuring out what you're even supposed to be doing. Two, we've historically been pretty bad at predicting which capabilities are hard. People thought the bottleneck would be reasoning, and it turned out that was easier than reliability and not making dumb mistakes in long chains of actions.

So I guess the way I'd frame it is less as a single date and more as a distribution over gradual diffusion. I think we'll see something that looks like a drop-in replacement for a narrow set of well-scoped remote roles fairly soon, and the share of roles that falls into that bucket expands over time as the horizon length grows and as the tooling and infrastructure around these systems gets built out. The thing I'd caution against is assuming that once the model is capable, the economic transition happens immediately. There's a lot of friction in how organizations adopt things, and integration takes real time. But I think the underlying trend is strong enough that it's worth taking the shorter timelines seriously rather than dismissing them.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts a demanding, broadly autonomous worker with replacement in a narrow set of well-scoped roles, but it does not distinguish replacing workers on every remotely performable task from replacing them on most such tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish between AI being able to do most of the tasks a remote worker does and being a drop-in replacement for that worker. Those could happen at quite different times.

A drop-in replacement is a pretty demanding standard. You need to be able to give it access to the tools your employee uses, explain what you want accomplished, and trust it to make progress without constantly checking its work. It needs to recognize when it’s missing information, ask useful questions, and recover when something goes wrong. Being very good at a well-specified task doesn’t establish that it can do all of that.

The thing I’d watch is the length of time over which these systems can reliably act autonomously. Can they complete something that would take a person an hour? A day? A week? And can they do that on the messy tasks people actually encounter at work, where success isn’t necessarily easy to verify?

I’d expect substantial economic effects before we reach the full drop-in replacement threshold. You can reorganize work around the capabilities the systems do have. So I’m more confident that AI will automate a growing share of remote work than I am about a particular date when you can substitute it for an employee without changing anything else.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes doing most of a worker’s tasks from being a drop-in replacement, but it does not identify the contrasting standard as replacing the worker on every remotely performable task.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between being able to do a task and being able to do a job. A model might perform very well on a task that takes a human an hour, especially if you give it a clear specification and an easy way to check whether it succeeded. But a remote worker has to figure out what needs doing, ask for clarification, deal with unexpected problems, and keep making progress over days or weeks.

So I’d look at the length of time over which these systems can reliably operate without someone intervening. Can you delegate something that would take a person a day? A week? And how much supervision do you need to provide? If you’re constantly checking the output and getting the system back on track, you haven’t really replaced the worker, even if the system is doing most of the typing.

That makes me somewhat cautious about identifying a particular benchmark score with a date for replacement. You need both the underlying capabilities and the reliability to put them together across a much longer sequence of decisions. I’d expect that to happen at different times for different jobs, with fairly substantial economic effects before we have something you could drop into almost any remote role.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes task ability from job-level reliability and notes that replacement will vary by job, but it does not distinguish replacement on every remotely performable task from replacement on most such tasks.
